overall_summary: Space and exoplanet content, particularly extreme planetary conditions and 'What If' survival scenarios, vastly outperform psychology and basic biology facts. Viewers are highly responsive to vivid, extreme cosmic hazards and sensory curiosity in deep space.

winning_patterns.pattern: Extreme Exoplanet Survival Scenarios ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (951 views) and 'What If You Fell Into This $26 Nonillion Diamond Planet?' (492 views) show high traction and strong engagement.
winning_patterns.action: Create a dedicated series of high-stakes survival scenarios set on the universe's most hostile planets, using first-person perspective hooks.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice...' (1,055 views), 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (1,025 views), and 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' (368 views) demonstrate strong baseline interest.
winning_patterns.action: Hook viewers with sensory anomalies (smells, tastes, extreme sights) in deep space to trigger immediate curiosity.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (multiple uploads getting 5-10 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently underperform.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize general cognitive psychology facts unless they can be tied to a highly visual, shocking, or cinematic mystery.

next_video.concept: What If You Fell Into the Planet of Screaming Glass?
next_video.opening_direction: Show a cinematic render of a beautiful deep blue planet, then immediately transition to a first-person POV of falling through a storm of razor-sharp shards.
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the winds blow at 5,400 miles per hour, meaning the glass rain doesn't fall down—it slices horizontally at seven times the speed of sound, shredding anything in seconds.
next_video.reason: Combines the highly successful 'What If You Fell Into...' format with the extreme planetary weather angle that generated over 1,000 views on similar concepts.

experiment: Test a 'Cinematic Animal Survival' short comparing prehistoric ocean predators to modern ones, leveraging the moderate success of the shark facts (302 views) but applying a high-intensity narrative structure.
